source: PGC1α and Pparγ are positive regulators of skeletal muscle differentiation (Haralampieva et al., 2017; Ruas et al., 2012; Singh et al., 2007), suggesting that the LRRC8A-dependent defect in skeletal muscle differentiation lies downstream of PGC1α and PPARγ.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Haralampieva et al., 2017; Ruas et al., 2012; Singh et al., 2007.

claim: The LRRC8A-dependent defect in skeletal muscle differentiation lies downstream of PGC1α and PPARγ.
source: PGC1α and Pparγ are positive regulators of skeletal muscle differentiation (Haralampieva et al., 2017; Ruas et al., 2012; Singh et al., 2007), suggesting that the LRRC8A-dependent defect in skeletal muscle differentiation lies downstream of PGC1α and PPARγ.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that PGC1α and PPARγ are induced in Lrrc8a KO myotubes despite impaired differentiation.

claim: Numerous signaling pathways essential for myogenic differentiation are disrupted in Lrrc8a KO C2C12 myotubes, including insulin, MAP kinase, PI3K-AKT, AMPK, integrin, mTOR, integrin linked kinase and IL-8 signaling pathways.
source: We found that numerous signaling pathways essential for myogenic differentiation are disrupted, including insulin (2 × 10−3), MAP kinase (5 × 10−4), PI3K-AKT (1 × 10−4), AMPK (6 × 10−5), integrin (3 × 10−6), mTOR (2 × 10−6), integrin linked kinase (4 × 10−7) and IL-8 (1 × 10−7) signaling pathways (Figure 1F and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1F and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Insulin-stimulated pAKT2 is abrogated in Lrrc8a KO myotubes compared to WT C2C12 myotubes.
source: Indeed, insulin-stimulated pAKT2, pAS160, pFOXO1 and pAMPK are abrogated in Lrrc8a KO myotubes compared to WT C2C12 myotubes (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: Insulin-stimulated pAS160 is abrogated in Lrrc8a KO myotubes compared to WT C2C12 myotubes.
source: Indeed, insulin-stimulated pAKT2, pAS160, pFOXO1 and pAMPK are abrogated in Lrrc8a KO myotubes compared to WT C2C12 myotubes (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: Insulin-stimulated pFOXO1 is abrogated in Lrrc8a KO myotubes compared to WT C2C12 myotubes.
source: Indeed, insulin-stimulated pAKT2, pAS160, pFOXO1 and pAMPK are abrogated in Lrrc8a KO myotubes compared to WT C2C12 myotubes (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: Insulin-stimulated pAMPK is abrogated in Lrrc8a KO myotubes compared to WT C2C12 myotubes.
source: Indeed, insulin-stimulated pAKT2, pAS160, pFOXO1 and pAMPK are abrogated in Lrrc8a KO myotubes compared to WT C2C12 myotubes (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: Insulin-AKT-AS160 signaling is diminished in Lrrc8a KO primary skeletal muscle myotubes compared to WT primary myotubes.
source: Importantly, insulin-AKT-AS160 signaling is also diminished in Lrrc8a KO primary skeletal muscle myotubes compared to WT primary myotubes (Figure 2B and D), consistent with the observed differentiation block (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: LRRC8A-dependent insulin-AKT and downstream signaling is conserved in primary skeletal myotubes.
source: Importantly, insulin-AKT-AS160 signaling is also diminished in Lrrc8a KO primary skeletal muscle myotubes compared to WT primary myotubes (Figure 2B and D), consistent with the observed differentiation block (Figure 1C). This confirms that LRRC8A-dependent insulin-AKT and downstream signaling is not a feature specific to immortalized C2C12 myotubes but is also conserved in primary skeletal myotubes.
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing similar effects in both C2C12 and primary myotubes (Figure 2A-D).

claim: Reduction in total AKT2 protein is associated with Lrrc8a ablation in both C2C12 and primary skeletal muscle cells.
source: It is also notable that reduction in total AKT2 protein is associated with Lrrc8a ablation in both C2C12 and primary skeletal muscle cells, and this is consistent with threefold reduction in AKT2 mRNA expression observed in RNA sequencing data (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data (Figure 2A, 2B) and RNA sequencing data (Figure 2E).

claim: AKT2 mRNA expression is reduced threefold in Lrrc8a KO C2C12 myotubes compared to WT.
source: It is also notable that reduction in total AKT2 protein is associated with Lrrc8a ablation in both C2C12 and primary skeletal muscle cells, and this is consistent with threefold reduction in AKT2 mRNA expression observed in RNA sequencing data (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Transcription of GLUT4 (Slc2a4) is suppressed 51-fold by Lrrc8a ablation.
source: Moreover, transcription of a number of critical insulin signaling and glucose homeostatic genes are suppressed by Lrrc8a ablation, including GLUT4 (Slc2a4 , 51-fold), FOXO3 (2-fold), FOXO4 (2.8-fold) and FOXO6 (18-fold) (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Transcription of FOXO3 is suppressed 2-fold by Lrrc8a ablation.
source: Moreover, transcription of a number of critical insulin signaling and glucose homeostatic genes are suppressed by Lrrc8a ablation, including GLUT4 (Slc2a4 , 51-fold), FOXO3 (2-fold), FOXO4 (2.8-fold) and FOXO6 (18-fold) (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Transcription of FOXO4 is suppressed 2.8-fold by Lrrc8a ablation.
source: Moreover, transcription of a number of critical insulin signaling and glucose homeostatic genes are suppressed by Lrrc8a ablation, including GLUT4 (Slc2a4 , 51-fold), FOXO3 (2-fold), FOXO4 (2.8-fold) and FOXO6 (18-fold) (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Transcription of FOXO6 is suppressed 18-fold by Lrrc8a ablation.
source: Moreover, transcription of a number of critical insulin signaling and glucose homeostatic genes are suppressed by Lrrc8a ablation, including GLUT4 (Slc2a4 , 51-fold), FOXO3 (2-fold), FOXO4 (2.8-fold) and FOXO6 (18-fold) (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: FOXO signaling integrates insulin signaling with glucose metabolism in insulin sensitive tissues.
source: Indeed, FOXO signaling is thought to integrate insulin signaling with glucose metabolism (Lee and Dong, 2017; Gross et al., 2008) in a number of insulin sensitive tissues.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lee and Dong, 2017; Gross et al., 2008.

claim: Impaired LRRC8A-dependent insulin-AKT-AS160-FOXO signaling is associated with the observed defect in myogenic differentiation upon Lrrc8a ablation in cultured skeletal myotubes.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that impaired LRRC8A-dependent insulin-AKT-AS160-FOXO signaling is associated with the observed defect in myogenic differentiation upon Lrrc8a ablation in cultured skeletal myotubes, and also predict putative impairments in skeletal muscle glucose metabolism and oxidative metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlation between impaired signaling and differentiation defects.

claim: Impaired LRRC8A-dependent insulin-AKT-AS160-FOXO signaling predicts putative impairments in skeletal muscle glucose metabolism and oxidative metabolism.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that impaired LRRC8A-dependent insulin-AKT-AS160-FOXO signaling is associated with the observed defect in myogenic differentiation upon Lrrc8a ablation in cultured skeletal myotubes, and also predict putative impairments in skeletal muscle glucose metabolism and oxidative metabolism.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the observed signaling impairments and gene expression changes.

claim: Impaired insulin signaling observed in LRRC8A-depleted myotubes is in part due to impaired myotube differentiation with secondary effects on insulin signaling.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that impaired insulin signaling observed in LRRC8A-depleted myotubes is in part due to impaired myotube differentiation with secondary effects on insulin signaling, and in part due to a direct contribution of LRRC8A to intracellular signaling in fully differentiated myotubes.
evidence: This is an inference based on experiments showing effects both before and after differentiation (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Impaired insulin signaling observed in LRRC8A-depleted myotubes is in part due to a direct contribution of LRRC8A to intracellular signaling in fully differentiated myotubes.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that impaired insulin signaling observed in LRRC8A-depleted myotubes is in part due to impaired myotube differentiation with secondary effects on insulin signaling, and in part due to a direct contribution of LRRC8A to intracellular signaling in fully differentiated myotubes.
evidence: This is an inference based on experiments showing effects in fully differentiated myotubes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: LRRC8A O/E to 2.12-fold WT levels fully rescues myotube development in Lrrc8a KO myotubes.
source: LRRC8A O/E to 2.12-fold WT levels fully rescues myotube development in Lrrc8a KO myotubes (Figure 3A), as quantified by restoration of Lrrc8a KO myotube area to levels above WT (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy and myotube area measurements shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: LRRC8A O/E restores Lrrc8a KO myotube area to levels above WT.
source: LRRC8A O/E to 2.12-fold WT levels fully rescues myotube development in Lrrc8a KO myotubes (Figure 3A), as quantified by restoration of Lrrc8a KO myotube area to levels above WT (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by myotube area measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Rescue of Lrrc8a KO myotube development upon LRRC8A O/E is associated with either restored or supra-normal signaling compared to WT C2C12 myotubes.
source: This rescue of Lrrc8a KO myotube development upon LRRC8A O/E (Figure 3A&B) is associated with either restored (pAS160, AKT2, pAKT1, AKT1, p70S6K) or supra-normal (pAKT2, p-p70S6K, pS6K, pERK1/2) signaling (Figure 3C&D) compared to WT C2C12 myotubes.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: LRRC8A protein expression level strongly regulates skeletal muscle insulin signaling and myogenic differentiation.
source: These data demonstrate that LRRC8A protein expression level strongly regulates skeletal muscle insulin signaling and myogenic differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dose-dependent effects of LRRC8A expression on signaling and differentiation (Figure 3).

claim: VRAC and the LRRC8A complex that functionally encodes it is mechano-responsive.
source: In a cellular context, there are numerous reports that VRAC and the LRRC8A complex that functionally encodes it is mechano-responsive (Browe and Baumgarten, 2003; Browe and Baumgarten, 2006; Osei-Owusu et al., 2018; Barakat et al., 1999; Nakao et al., 1999; Nilius and Droogmans, 2001; Romanenko et al., 2002; Strange et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Browe and Baumgarten, 2003; Browe and Baumgarten, 2006; Osei-Owusu et al., 2018; Barakat et al., 1999; Nakao et al., 1999; Nilius and Droogmans, 2001; Romanenko et al., 2002; Strange et al., 2019.

claim: Mechanical stretch is an important regulator of skeletal muscle proliferation, differentiation and skeletal muscle hypertrophy.
source: It is well established that mechanical stretch is an important regulator of skeletal muscle proliferation, differentiation and skeletal muscle hypertrophy and may be mediated by PI3K-AKT-MAPK signaling (Schiaffino et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2018) and integrin signaling pathways (Carson and Wei, 2000; Schlaepfer et al., 1999; Flück et al., 1999; Klossner et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Schiaffino et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2018; Carson and Wei, 2000; Schlaepfer et al., 1999; Flück et al., 1999; Klossner et al., 2009.

claim: Mechanical stretch may regulate skeletal muscle proliferation, differentiation and hypertrophy via PI3K-AKT-MAPK signaling.
source: It is well established that mechanical stretch is an important regulator of skeletal muscle proliferation, differentiation and skeletal muscle hypertrophy and may be mediated by PI3K-AKT-MAPK signaling (Schiaffino et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2018) and integrin signaling pathways (Carson and Wei, 2000; Schlaepfer et al., 1999; Flück et al., 1999; Klossner et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Schiaffino et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2018.

claim: Mechanical stretch may regulate skeletal muscle proliferation, differentiation and hypertrophy via integrin signaling pathways.
source: It is well established that mechanical stretch is an important regulator of skeletal muscle proliferation, differentiation and skeletal muscle hypertrophy and may be mediated by PI3K-AKT-MAPK signaling (Schiaffino et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2018) and integrin signaling pathways (Carson and Wei, 2000; Schlaepfer et al., 1999; Flück et al., 1999; Klossner et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Carson and Wei, 2000; Schlaepfer et al., 1999; Flück et al., 1999; Klossner et al., 2009.

claim: Mechanical stretch (5%) is sufficient to stimulate PI3K-AKT2/AKT1-pAS160-MAPK (ERK1/2) signaling in WT C2C12 in a LRRC8A-dependent manner.
source: Mechanical stretch (5%) is sufficient to stimulate PI3K-AKT2/AKT1-pAS160-MAPK (ERK1/2) signaling in WT C2C12 in a LRRC8A-dependent manner (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing stretch-induced signaling in WT but not Lrrc8a KO myotubes (Figure 4A and B).

claim: LRRC8A is a co-regulator of both insulin and stretch-mediated PI3K-AKT-pAS160-MAPK signaling.
source: These data position LRRC8A as a co-regulator of both insulin and stretch-mediated PI3K-AKT- pAS160-MAPK signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data showing LRRC8A regulates both insulin-stimulated (Figure 2) and stretch-stimulated (Figure 4) signaling.

claim: The LRRC8A complex interacts with GRB2 in lymphocytes and regulates PI3K-AKT signaling.
source: It has been reported earlier in both lymphocyte and adipocytes that the LRRC8A complex interacts with Growth factor Receptor-Bound 2 (GRB2) and regulates PI3K-AKT signaling (Kumar et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017; Gunasekar et al., 2019), whereby GRB2 binds with IRS1/2 and negatively regulates insulin signaling (Shan et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kumar et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017; Gunasekar et al., 2019.

claim: The LRRC8A complex interacts with GRB2 in adipocytes and regulates PI3K-AKT signaling.
source: It has been reported earlier in both lymphocyte and adipocytes that the LRRC8A complex interacts with Growth factor Receptor-Bound 2 (GRB2) and regulates PI3K-AKT signaling (Kumar et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017; Gunasekar et al., 2019), whereby GRB2 binds with IRS1/2 and negatively regulates insulin signaling (Shan et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kumar et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017; Gunasekar et al., 2019.

claim: GRB2 binds with IRS1/2 and negatively regulates insulin signaling.
source: It has been reported earlier in both lymphocyte and adipocytes that the LRRC8A complex interacts with Growth factor Receptor-Bound 2 (GRB2) and regulates PI3K-AKT signaling (Kumar et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017; Gunasekar et al., 2019), whereby GRB2 binds with IRS1/2 and negatively regulates insulin signaling (Shan et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Shan et al., 2013.

claim: GRB2 knock-down augments insulin-PI3K-MAPK signaling and induces myogenesis and myogenic differentiation genes.
source: Indeed, GRB2 knock-down augments insulin-PI3K-MAPK signaling and induces myogenesis and myogenic differentiation genes (Shan et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2009; Mitra and Thanabalu, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Shan et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2009; Mitra and Thanabalu, 2017.

claim: LRRC8A and GRB2 interact in C2C12 myotubes.
source: To determine if LRRC8A and GRB2 interact in C2C12 myotubes, we overexpressed C-terminal 3XFlag tagged LRRC8A in C2C12 cells followed by immunoprecipitation (IP) with Flag antibody. We observed significant GRB2 enrichment upon Flag IP from lysates of LRRC8A-3xFlag expressing C2C12 myotubes, consistent with a GRB2-LRRC8A interaction (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data showing GRB2 enrichment upon Flag IP (Figure 5A).

claim: GRB2 knock-down rescues myotube formation in Lrrc8a KO C2C12 myotubes.
source: shRNA-mediated GRB2 KD in Lrrc8a KO C2C12 myoblasts ( LRRC8A KO/shGRB2; Figure 5B) stimulates myotube formation (Figure 5C) and increases myotube area (Figure 5D), to levels equivalent to WT/shSCR (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy and myotube area measurements shown in Figure 5B, 5C, and 5D.

claim: GRB2 knock-down in Lrrc8a KO C2C12 myotubes induces myogenic differentiation markers IGF1, MyoHCl, MyoHClla and MyoHCIIb relative to both LRRC8A KO/shSCR and WT/shSCR.
source: Similarly, GRB2 KD in Lrrc8a KO C2C12 myotubes induces myogenic differentiation markers IGF1, MyoHCl, MyoHClla and MyoHCIIb relative to both LRRC8A KO/shSCR and WT/shSCR (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: GRB2 suppression rescues myotube differentiation in Lrrc8a KO C2C12.
source: These data are consistent with GRB2 suppression rescuing myotube differentiation in Lrrc8a KO C2C12, and supports a model in which LRRC8A regulates myogenic differentiation by titrating GRB2-mediated signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: LRRC8A regulates myogenic differentiation by titrating GRB2-mediated signaling.
source: These data are consistent with GRB2 suppression rescuing myotube differentiation in Lrrc8a KO C2C12, and supports a model in which LRRC8A regulates myogenic differentiation by titrating GRB2-mediated signaling.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the interaction between LRRC8A and GRB2, and the rescue of differentiation upon GRB2 knockdown (Figure 5).

claim: Skm KO mice develop skeletal muscle mass comparable to WT littermates based on Echo/MRI body composition.
source: Remarkably, in contrast to the severe impairments in skeletal myogenesis observed in both Lrrc8a KO C2C12 and primary skeletal myotubes in vitro (Figures 1, 3 and 5), Skm KO mice develop skeletal muscle mass comparable to WT littermates, based on Echo/MRI body composition (Figure 6C) and gross muscle weights (Figure 6D), and are born at normal mendelian ratios (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by body composition data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Skm KO mice develop skeletal muscle mass comparable to WT littermates based on gross muscle weights.
source: Remarkably, in contrast to the severe impairments in skeletal myogenesis observed in both Lrrc8a KO C2C12 and primary skeletal myotubes in vitro (Figures 1, 3 and 5), Skm KO mice develop skeletal muscle mass comparable to WT littermates, based on Echo/MRI body composition (Figure 6C) and gross muscle weights (Figure 6D), and are born at normal mendelian ratios (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by muscle weight data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Skm KO mice are born at normal mendelian ratios.
source: Remarkably, in contrast to the severe impairments in skeletal myogenesis observed in both Lrrc8a KO C2C12 and primary skeletal myotubes in vitro (Figures 1, 3 and 5), Skm KO mice develop skeletal muscle mass comparable to WT littermates, based on Echo/MRI body composition (Figure 6C) and gross muscle weights (Figure 6D), and are born at normal mendelian ratios (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by breeding data shown in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Histological examination reveals a 27% reduction in skeletal myocyte cross-sectional area in Skm KO as compared to WT mice.
source: However, histological examination reveals a 27% reduction in skeletal myocyte cross-sectional area in Skm KO as compared to WT mice (Figure 6E), suggesting a requirement for LRRC8A in skeletal muscle cell size regulation in vivo.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: LRRC8A is required for skeletal muscle cell size regulation in vivo.
source: However, histological examination reveals a 27% reduction in skeletal myocyte cross-sectional area in Skm KO as compared to WT mice (Figure 6E), suggesting a requirement for LRRC8A in skeletal muscle cell size regulation in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed reduction in myocyte cross-sectional area in Skm KO mice (Figure 6E).

claim: The reduction in skeletal myocyte cross-sectional area in Skm KO mice is potentially due to reductions in myotube fusion.
source: This is potentially due to reductions in myotube fusion, as observed in C2C12 and primary skeletal muscle cells in vitro (Figure 1), but occurring to a lesser degree in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative statement indicated by the word 'potentially', based on inference from in vitro observations.

claim: The profound impairments in myogenesis observed in vitro may reflect a very early requirement for LRRC8A signaling in skeletal muscle development prior to LRRC8A protein elimination by Myf5-Cre-mediated LRRC8A recombination.
source: These data indicate that the profound impairments in myogenesis observed in vitro may reflect a very early requirement for LRRC8A signaling in skeletal muscle development (prior to LRRC8A protein elimination by Myf5-Cre-mediated LRRC8A recombination), or other fundamental differences in myogenic differentiation processes in vitro versus in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative statement indicated by the word 'may', based on inference from the discordance between in vitro and in vivo phenotypes.

claim: The profound impairments in myogenesis observed in vitro may reflect fundamental differences in myogenic differentiation processes in vitro versus in vivo.
source: These data indicate that the profound impairments in myogenesis observed in vitro may reflect a very early requirement for LRRC8A signaling in skeletal muscle development (prior to LRRC8A protein elimination by Myf5-Cre-mediated LRRC8A recombination), or other fundamental differences in myogenic differentiation processes in vitro versus in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative statement indicated by the word 'may', based on inference from the discordance between in vitro and in vivo phenotypes.

claim: Insulin signaling is an important regulator of skeletal muscle oxidative capacity and endurance.
source: Since insulin signaling is an important regulator of skeletal muscle oxidative capacity and endurance (Affourtit, 2016), we next examined exercise tolerance on treadmill testing in Lrrc8afl/fl (WT) compared to Skm KO .
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Affourtit, 2016.

claim: Skm KO mice exhibit a 14% reduced exercise capacity compared to age and gender matched WT controls.
source: Skm KO mice exhibit a 14% reduced exercise capacity, compared to age and gender matched WT controls (Figure 7A; Figure 7—Video 1).
evidence: Supported by treadmill testing data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Hang-times on inversion testing are reduced 29% in Skm KO compared to controls.
source: Hang-times on inversion testing are also reduced 29% in Skm KO compared to controls, further supporting reduced skeletal muscle endurance upon skeletal muscle LRRC8A depletion in vivo (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by inversion testing data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Peak developed tetanic tension is 15% reduced in Skm KO soleus muscle compared to WT controls.
source: We observed that peak developed tetanic tension is 15% reduced in Skm KO soleus muscle compared to WT controls (Figure 7C), suggesting a skeletal muscle autonomous mechanism, with no difference in time to fatigability (TTF, Figure 7D) or time to 50% decay (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by ex vivo muscle testing data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The reduction in force generation in Skm KO soleus muscle suggests a skeletal muscle autonomous mechanism.
source: We observed that peak developed tetanic tension is 15% reduced in Skm KO soleus muscle compared to WT controls (Figure 7C), suggesting a skeletal muscle autonomous mechanism, with no difference in time to fatigability (TTF, Figure 7D) or time to 50% decay (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the ex vivo muscle testing showing intrinsic muscle defects (Figure 7C).

claim: There is no difference in time to fatigability between Skm KO and WT soleus muscle.
source: We observed that peak developed tetanic tension is 15% reduced in Skm KO soleus muscle compared to WT controls (Figure 7C), suggesting a skeletal muscle autonomous mechanism, with no difference in time to fatigability (TTF, Figure 7D) or time to 50% decay (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by ex vivo muscle testing data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: There is no difference in time to 50% decay between Skm KO and WT soleus muscle.
source: We observed that peak developed tetanic tension is 15% reduced in Skm KO soleus muscle compared to WT controls (Figure 7C), suggesting a skeletal muscle autonomous mechanism, with no difference in time to fatigability (TTF, Figure 7D) or time to 50% decay (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by ex vivo muscle testing data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Oxygen consumption of Lrrc8a KO primary myotubes are 26% lower than WT.
source: Oxygen consumption of Lrrc8a KO primary myotubes are 26% lower than WT and, in contrast to WT cells, are unresponsive to insulin-stimulation (Figure 7F), consistent with abrogation of insulin-AKT/ERK1/2 signaling upon skeletal muscle LRRC8A depletion.
evidence: Supported by Seahorse assay data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Lrrc8a KO primary myotubes are unresponsive to insulin-stimulation in terms of oxygen consumption.
source: Oxygen consumption of Lrrc8a KO primary myotubes are 26% lower than WT and, in contrast to WT cells, are unresponsive to insulin-stimulation (Figure 7F), consistent with abrogation of insulin-AKT/ERK1/2 signaling upon skeletal muscle LRRC8A depletion.
evidence: Supported by Seahorse assay data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: FCCP abolishes differences in oxygen consumption between WT and Lrrc8a KO primary muscle cells, suggesting no differences in functional mitochondrial content in Lrrc8a KO muscle.
source: In contrast, FCCP, which maximally uncouples mitochondria, abolishes differences in oxygen consumption between WT and Lrrc8a KO primary muscle cells, suggesting no differences in functional mitochondrial content in Lrrc8a KO muscle.
evidence: This is an inference based on Seahorse assay data showing similar maximal oxygen consumption after FCCP treatment (Figure 7F).

claim: There are no differences in muscle fiber-type in Skm KO as compared to WT mice.
source: Consistent with this finding, we observe no differences in muscle fiber-type based on Myosin Heavy Chain (MHC) Type 1, MHC Type IIa, MHC Type IIx and MHC Type IIb in both superficial and deep tibialis anterior muscle in Skm KO as compared to WT mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), indicating the reductions in muscle force and endurance in Skm KO mice is not due to muscle fiber-type switching.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reductions in muscle force and endurance in Skm KO mice is not due to muscle fiber-type switching.
source: Consistent with this finding, we observe no differences in muscle fiber-type based on Myosin Heavy Chain (MHC) Type 1, MHC Type IIa, MHC Type IIx and MHC Type IIb in both superficial and deep tibialis anterior muscle in Skm KO as compared to WT mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), indicating the reductions in muscle force and endurance in Skm KO mice is not due to muscle fiber-type switching.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of no differences in muscle fiber-type (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Changes in muscle metabolic potential and morphology may occur independent from adaptive fiber-type switching as measured by a change in MHC expression.
source: Indeed, it is increasingly appreciated that changes in muscle metabolic potential and morphology may occur independent from adaptive fiber-type switching as measured by a change in MHC expression (Egan and Zierath, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Egan and Zierath, 2013.

claim: Insulin-stimulated ECAR increases are abolished in Lrrc8a KO compared to WT cells.
source: Insulin-stimulated ECAR increases are abolished in Lrrc8a KO compared to WT cells, and these differences persist independent of electron transport chain modulators (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse ECAR data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: LRRC8A regulation of skeletal muscle cellular oxygen consumption occurs at the level of glucose metabolism.
source: These data suggest that LRRC8A regulation of skeletal muscle cellular oxygen consumption occurs at the level of glucose metabolism - potentially via LRRC8A-dependent insulin-PI3K-AKT-AS160-GLUT4 signaling, glucose uptake and utilization.
evidence: This is an inference based on ECAR and OCR data (Figure 7F, 7H).

claim: LRRC8A regulation of skeletal muscle cellular oxygen consumption potentially occurs via LRRC8A-dependent insulin-PI3K-AKT-AS160-GLUT4 signaling, glucose uptake and utilization.
source: These data suggest that LRRC8A regulation of skeletal muscle cellular oxygen consumption occurs at the level of glucose metabolism - potentially via LRRC8A-dependent insulin-PI3K-AKT-AS160-GLUT4 signaling, glucose uptake and utilization.
evidence: This is a speculative statement indicated by the word 'potentially', based on inference from signaling and metabolic data.

claim: Lrrc8a ablation in C2C12 myotubes results in marked transcriptional suppression of numerous glycolytic genes: Aldoa, Eno3, Pfkm, and Pgam2.
source: These findings in primary skeletal muscle cells are supported by marked transcriptional suppression of numerous glycolytic genes: Aldoa, Eno3, Pfkm, and Pgam2; and glucose and glycogen metabolism genes: Phka1, Phka2, Ppp1r3c and Gys1, upon Lrrc8a ablation in C2C12 myotubes (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Lrrc8a ablation in C2C12 myotubes results in marked transcriptional suppression of glucose and glycogen metabolism genes: Phka1, Phka2, Ppp1r3c and Gys1.
source: These findings in primary skeletal muscle cells are supported by marked transcriptional suppression of numerous glycolytic genes: Aldoa, Eno3, Pfkm, and Pgam2; and glucose and glycogen metabolism genes: Phka1, Phka2, Ppp1r3c and Gys1, upon Lrrc8a ablation in C2C12 myotubes (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
